⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that theraguns are the gold standard for massage guns; the brand name has come to be synonymous with the entire product category, much like “Kleenex” is for tissues.
  • I haven't yet tried every product in the Therabody lineup (I’m getting there), but I've put most to the test and am ready to recommend my favorites.
  • Need more gift ideas for the active person in your life?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that theraguns are the gold standard for massage guns; the brand name has come to be synonymous with the entire product category, much like “Kleenex” is for tissues. But Therabody, the innovative tech giant behind Theragun, offers more than relief for sore muscles and pain. It now sells a broad repertoire of wellness gadgets aimed at alleviating ailments like eye strain, menstrual cramps, and skin puffiness (to name a few). So whether you’re shopping for a fitness lover or someone who could use a little self-care, there’s likely a Therabody gadget worth wrapping up.

I haven't yet tried every product in the Therabody lineup (I’m getting there), but I've put most to the test and am ready to recommend my favorites. Plus, most are FSA/HSA-eligible and designed with USB-C charging capability.

Need more gift ideas for the active person in your life? Check out our guides to the Best Massage Guns, Best Massagers, and Best Compression Boots.

In a recent development, updated November 2026: I’ve added the Theragun Prime (6th Gen) and removed discontinued products. I also confirmed up-to-date links and prices.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Sources indicate that if you’re looking for a professional-grade massage device, the Theragun Pro Plus is one of the most advanced percussive guns on the market, incorporating vibrations, heat, and near-infrared LED therapies for an all-in-one recovery tool. It also offers cold therapy, but you'll have to purchase an additional attachment for $100 to make use of that capability—a steep add-on for what is already a splurge. After testing the attachment myself, I don't think it justifies the cost unless you are sure you'd regularly use the contrast therapy.

Industry observers note that priced at $650, this is the most expensive Theragun, so I'd recommend it to athletes or those who are dealing with chronic muscle pain and want the LED therapy. For casual users, some of the features might feel like overkill. For example, there's a built-in biometric sensor for heart rate tracking that I have barely used. I do, though, appreciate the OLED screen, which displays a force meter, so you can see exactly how much pressure you're applying. It's a useful function if you need a nudge to apply more pressure or a reminder to ease up.

Industry observers note that the Theragun Prime (6th Gen) hits the sweet spot between the elite Pro Plus and the budget-friendly Relief. It’s still a premium percussive massage gun, with five speed settings, two attachments (a dampener and standard ball), and up to 120 minutes of battery life. You won’t get extras like heated or near-infrared LED therapy, or compatibility with Therabody’s cold and vibration attachments, but you will enjoy top-notch durability. It’s the only Theragun in the lineup rated to withstand drops from up to 10 feet, making it an excellent gift for the accident-prone person in your life.

The Theragun Relief, rolled out in 2023, remains the cheapest Theragun—priced even lower than the Mini Plus. For the price tag, you’re sacrificing some of the premium features, like the LCD screen and Bluetooth connectivity to the Therabody app for device control. But you can still follow guided routines on the app, and the simple one-button control is refreshingly simple to use.

The Relief comes with three head attachments and has three speed settings, which is a step down from models that offer a standard five speeds and four or more attachments. Still, the Relief is less than half the weight of the Pro Plus, and it's equipped with the essentials, which is more than enough for the average person.

The original Theragun Mini is still a solid portable device—and it's $60 less—but the Mini Plus feels like a shrunken version of the elite Pro Plus. The ergonomic triangular design lets me target trigger points and muscle groups like my hamstrings and calves with more pressure control (though, admittedly, that same shape makes it awkward to use on my lower back). Thoughtful details, like a travel lock to prevent it from powering on and a compact carrying pouch, make it easy to carry on commutes and flights.

In a recent development, most notably, it brings heated percussive therapy to a travel-friendly device. The heat therapy is easily my favorite feature on the Pro Plus. The Mini Plus is also compatible with Therabody's Vibration Plus and Cold Plus attachments (both sold separately).

Recent findings suggest that note: Some customers have reported charging issues, saying their units wouldn't power up, but I haven't run into any battery problems in my two weeks of testing. I'll update this review if anything shifts with long-term use.

The JetBoots Pro Plus are full-length, wireless boots that combine pneumatic compression with vibration therapy and infrared LED light. Everything is controlled from a built-in LCD screen and control panel on the lead boot, and connectivity is effortless, automatically linking when powered on.

Eight preset programs target legs, knees, and joints, but you can manually adjust pressure, intensity, and the session length. Sessions can run from 10 to 60 minutes in five-minute increments, with compression adjustable between 20 and 100 millimeters of mercury (mmHg)—a standard unit of measurement for pressure. Vibration offers three intensity levels (low, medium, and high), and the infrared LED setting is a simple on or off, with an automatic shutoff after 45 minutes.

It has been revealed that inside the boots, a nonporous proprietary material reduces moisture and microbial buildup, and after months of testing, I haven't noticed any lingering odors. These are best suited for athletes, frequent travelers, or anyone managing circulation-related conditions. Conveniently for those aforementioned jet-setters, the JetBoots Pro Plus are TSA-approved for carry-on travel; just keep in mind that they're pretty hefty.

I enjoyed the original TheraFace Mask, but the upgraded TheraFace Mask Glo feels like the smarter purchase. It's easier to find (Therabody seems to be phasing out the original), costs $270 less, and is slightly lighter at 1.13 pounds versus the OG's 1.27 pounds. While the Glo has fewer LED bulbs—504 compared to 648—the difference doesn't translate to a lesser treatment. You get the same red, infrared, and blue light wavelengths, plus the signature vibration therapy that made the first-generation mask stand out.

The vibrations are now integrated into the adjustable straps rather than the mask itself. They're usually distracting, occasionally even headache-inducing, depending on my mood. I usually skip the vibration setting altogether to make this component less irritating. Even without it, the Glo remains competitively priced among high-end LED masks.

Treatment sessions range from four to 12 minutes, and the removable eye shields are thoughtful, but I prefer taking them off to extend the light coverage to my under-eye area. I very much appreciate the cordless design, but I do miss the display stand that came with the original. I often end up storing it back in its box, which makes me less inclined to reach for it. If you, too, deal with this problem, you might consider buying a travel case for $80.

Sources indicate that I challenge you to stay awake through a full session with the SmartGoggles 2.0. I’ve been testing them for months, and more often than not, I conk out while wearing them. The combination of gentle heat, vibration, and massage therapy across my forehead, eyebrows, and temples relaxes my facial tension within minutes. I love wearing them when I have a headache from staring at screens all day, and while I don’t struggle with regular migraines, I can see them being a soothing blackout remedy in a quiet, dark room.

According to recent reports, former reviewer Medea Giordano loved the first model, and this upgrade improves the fit with contoured padding that feels similar to Therabody’s SleepMask. You still get three preset modes: Focus, Sleep, and SmartRelax. That last option uses biometric feedback to adjust vibration patterns based on your heart rate. It also syncs with the Therabody app, letting you tweak the vibration and heat intensities or incorporate sound therapy. Note, though, if you’re a side-sleeper, you’ll have to shift around, as these are most comfortable while lying flat on your back.

Sources indicate that I’ve tested several sleep masks, and the TheraFace SleepMask is among my favorites. Many claim to be 100 percent blackout, but this one leaves me feeling totally disoriented when I wake up, with no idea what dimension I'm in—just how I like it. The contoured padding feels plush, and the adjustable strap keeps the mask in place without tugging at my hair, even when I shift around at night. It comes with a carrying case, so I always pack it for travel.

It has been revealed that the selling point is that this mask uses vibrations—three pattern presets (Pulse, Wave, Constant)—designed to nudge your brain into deeper rest. I struggle with staying asleep, but when I wake up in the middle of the night, I just tap the button to start a 15-minute session, and it usually lulls me back to sleep. That said, the vibrations are almost too gentle; you barely feel them, but you can absolutely hear them. It's not as soothing as a white noise machine, so if you're a light sleeper, this might be a deal-breaker.

The TheraFace Depuffing Wand has become a staple in my travel bag. It delivers both hot and cold therapy to help reduce puffiness, improve circulation, and enhance product absorption before completing your skin care routine. It’s TSA-friendly—zero awkward bag checks and counting—and ideal for tackling under-eye bags after a long flight or night. The curved applicator reaches every contour of my face, and the precision tip is great for trickier spots like under my eyes. It’s intended to be used on clean, dry skin, so I hold the opposite side of my face to prevent tugging.

The wand comes with three preset temperature levels that feel gentle but effective. While the cold function isn’t as icy as a roller fresh from the freezer, it’s consistent throughout a six-minute session and doesn’t drip. Plus, this one won’t crack if you forget to take it out of the freezer (RIP to two of my traditional rollers). An indicator light flashes at three minutes to remind you to switch sides, but this notification is easy to miss if you’re not looking straight into a mirror.

In a recent development, cupping is an ancient healing technique that uses suction to provide muscle relief. Therabody's version combines suction, heat, and vibration therapy for localized recovery. With three levels of suction (30, 40, and 50 kilopascals, or kPa), three heat intensities (41, 43, and 45 degrees Celsius), and three vibration modes (low, high, and wave), I appreciate how you can customize the intensity of your session. The TheraCup is also programmed with an auto-shutoff after three minutes—so you don’t overdo any area—and built-in safety sensors that will cut off the pressure if it exceeds 60 kPa.

It has been revealed that theraFace Mask for $650: The TheraFace Mask is a cordless, hands-free light-therapy device that uses three wavelengths (red, infrared, and blue) to tackle different skin care goals. As a distinguishing feature from its competitors, the TheraFace Mask includes a built-in vibration therapy mode that massages pressure points around the eyes, brow line, and scalp for some added stress relief. It comes with removable eye shields and a sleek display stand, which makes it easy to store on your nightstand.

In a recent development, jetBoots Prime for $550: Compared to the JetBoots Pro Plus, the JetBoots Prime is simple to use: You get four pressure levels (25, 50, 75, and 100 mmHg) and three durations (20, 40, or 60 minutes), all adjustable throughout your session through a built-in control panel. Th boots are wireless with a 180-minute battery life and can even be used while charging. Plus, they fold down into the included drawstring bag, making them portable and fuss-free to stow away.

WaveRoller for $180: Foam rollers are great for improving range of motion, increasing blood flow, and reducing muscle tension. You can buy a decent foam roller for significantly less, but with the WaveRoller, you get Therabody app integration for a personalized experience and five vibration frequencies. Designed for full-body use, it works best for warm-ups and post-workout recovery.

Theragun Mini (3rd Generation) for $220: I recommend the Mini if you’re latest to percussive therapy or need something packable for travel. It's the smallest and lightest Theragun, with three attachments (standard ball, dampener, and thumb) and a soft-zip case that fits into a tote, gym bag, or carry-on.

Recent findings suggest that theragun Sense for $300: The Theragun Sense is slightly smaller (and lighter) than the Pro Plus, and it’s also impressively quiet. Some settings are almost silent, allowing for a discreet recovery session at any time of day without worrying about bothering your housemates. It has the same LCD screen and breathwork features as the Pro Plus, too. The main difference here is that it's compatible with fewer attachments, but four heads are still more than enough for many active individuals.

I'll be testing the ThermFace Massage ($200), the ThermNeck & Upper Back ($380), RecoveryTherm Cube ($160), and the RecoveryPulse Arm ($160).

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

Google’s AI feature in Search gets its own incognito mode

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (437 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google’s search engine has long offered an incognito mode for all those search queries you don’t want logged or associated with your account.
  • Industry observers note that many leading AI chatbots already offer the option for temporary chats, Google Gemini included.
  • Recent findings suggest that google says that users won’t have to adjust their settings to take advantage of the new option.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google’s search engine has long offered an incognito mode for all those search queries you don’t want logged or associated with your account. Now, Google’s AI Mode in Search is getting a similar feature. In a blog post, the organization announced a new feature that brings “temporary threads” to AI Mode, where the conversations you have won’t be resurfaced later in areas like your search history or recommendations.

Industry observers note that many leading AI chatbots already offer the option for temporary chats, Google Gemini included. However, there was not yet an option to have a temporary chat when you’re searching Google and are dropped into its conversational interface, known as AI Mode.

Recent findings suggest that google says that users won’t have to adjust their settings to take advantage of the new option. Instead, they’ll be able to click a temporary threads icon in the upper right corner of AI Mode to engage in a temporary chat. This essentially works the same as a temporary chat would in the stand-alone Gemini chatbot.

The option could be convenient to use at those times when you start digging deeper into a particular topic via AI Mode and realize that you don’t want the discussion to become a part of your search history because of its personal nature.

In a recent development, once the temporary thread is started, the session becomes detached from your account, Google says. This means that the responses the AI provides won’t be informed by past preferences, nor will they impact future personalization. That could also be useful for those times when you want to learn about something as more of a one-off, but don’t want Google to start to think of the topic as one of your main interests.

When you close out of the thread, you will return to searching as usual.

The manufacturer notes the option to engage in temporary chats in AI Mode is rolling out globally on desktop and mobile across all supported languages.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2024-27834 Apple Multiple Products Improper Authentication Vulnerability This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not at the moment listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

US Government Partners Urge Hardening Industrial Refrigeration and Cold Chain Monitoring Systems

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1285 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cisa

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Overview The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Health and Human Services (HHS), U.S.
  • The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Health and Human Services (HHS), U.S.
  • The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to defend against this activity by using strong authentication, keeping systems updated, identifying any systems that are accessible from the internet, removing unnecessary remote access, and securing any necessary remote access.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Overview The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Health and Human Services (HHS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), and the Department of Transportation (DoT)—hereafter referred to as “the authoring organizations”—are aware of malicious cyber activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems globally. Organizations in the Healthcare and Public Health, Chemical, Food and Agriculture, and Transportation Systems Sectors widely use these systems, including in refrigerated transport services, for automated and remote monitoring of temperatures, continuous temperature logging, defrost cycle management, and energy optimization. The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to defend against this activity by using strong authentication, keeping systems updated, identifying any systems that are accessible from the internet, removing unnecessary remote access, and securing any necessary remote access. Threat The authoring organizations are aware of malicious cyber actors targeting electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities. The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards. Specifically, the actors may exploit these flaws through multiple vectors: Authentication bypass; Arbitrary code injection; and Weak configurations. Upon successful exploitation of the flaws, the actors could achieve the following effects: Change of temperature, which could: Affect the service life of the system; Create a fire hazard; Cause loss of inventory; or Indirectly harm consumers if products are consumed after unsafe storage. Loss of visibility into current temperatures (a denial-of-view condition). Mitigations The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to immediately take the following actions. These mitigations align with the Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals (CPGs), developed by CISA and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). The CPGs provide a minimum set of practices and protections that CISA and NIST recommend all organizations implement: Eliminate public internet exposure: Do not expose control system devices and/or systems, particularly controller panels, to the internet [CPG 3.S]. Should remote access be necessary, protect it by using a firewall or edge device and updating it to the latest version to reduce security vulnerabilities. See CISA’s Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance and Defend the Edge: The Critical Importance of Edge Device Security for additional guidance on securing edge devices. Isolate operational technology (OT) devices: Create a dedicated OT virtual local area network (VLAN) to separate OT devices from business networks [CPG 3.I]. Enforce credential security: Change default passwords [CPG 3.A], strengthen passwords, and implement strong password policies [CPG 3.B]. Further, implement phishing-resistant multifactor authentication wherever feasible [CPG 3.F]. Apply patches: Keep device firmware up to date and establish a structured lifecycle management process to identify, retire, and replace legacy devices that are at end of life (EOL) and no longer supported by the manufacturer [CPG 2.A, 2.B]. See CISA’s BOD 26-04: Implementation Guidance for Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk and BOD 26-02: Mitigating Risk From End-of-Support Edge Devices for additional guidance. Restrict access: Define and maintain device and IP address allowlisting, limiting access to only those devices and IP addresses authorized to make changes [CPG 3.H]. Have reliable backups: Maintain current backups offsite and offline and test them [CPG 3.O]. Monitor and report: Enable logging [CPG 3.Q] and regularly review logs for unexpected activity. For OT assets where logs are non-standard or not available, collect network traffic and communications between the assets. Review setpoint ranges: Define and maintain reasonable setpoint limits for devices operating downstream of controllers to stay within safe ranges and establish alerting for deviations. Resources The authoring organizations strongly urge industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring system owners and operators to secure remote access to their OT systems. To strengthen system security, owners and operators should review the following resources and implement recommended mitigations: CISA: Primary Mitigations to Reduce Cyber Threats to Operational Technology CISA: Defend the Edge: The Critical Importance of Edge Device Security CISA: Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance United Kingdom’s National Cyber Security Centre and Partners: Secure Connectivity Principles for OT Contact Information The authoring organizations recommend U.S. organizations report suspicious or criminal activity related to information provided in this fact sheet: Contact CISA via CISA’s 24/7 Operations Center at contact@cisa.dhs.gov or 1-844-Say-CISA (1-844-729-2472). For more information on reporting a cyber incident, refer to CISA’s Voluntary Cyber Incident Reporting web page. File a claim with FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) or contact your local FBI field office. When available, please include the following information regarding the incident: Date, time, and location of the incident; Type of activity; Number of people affected; Type of equipment used for the activity; and Name of the submitting firm or organization, and a designated point of contact. Contact HHS via HHSCyber@hhs.gov or the HHS 24/7 Operations Center at 202-619-7800 for assistance mitigating potential disruptions to the delivery of healthcare resulting from health and medical supply chain impacts. Industry observers note that U.K.-based fintech Payhawk announced a $280 million Series C funding round Wednesday, led by Goldman Sachs’ growth equity arm, making it one of Europe’s largest Series C rounds this year, as noted by Sifted. The round values the firm at $2 billion, bringing its total funding to more than $500 million to date.

Founded in 2018, Payhawk is an enterprise financial management platform that helps companies track and manage expenses and procurement using AI agents. Speaking to FinTech magazine, Payhawk’s co-founder and CEO, Hristo Borisov, stated the company saw “an incredible growth opportunity and room to bring finance teams AI-native products that combine agents, payment infrastructure, and enterprise controls.”.

According to recent reports, payhawk competes with spend management companies Pleo, Moss, and Spendesk, and indicates it operates in 33 countries. Notably, the tech giant stated it still has 70% of the $100 million it raised in 2022, a round that valued the company at $1 billion. This fresh capital will support its global expansion. Other investors in the round include Greenoaks, Lightspeed, and QED.

Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1987 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document.
  • Token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors.
  • Industry observers note that in this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document. This makes them wonderfully expressive for search, but those document vectors add up quickly. A corpus with millions of documents can contain hundreds of millions of vectors!

Token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors. The more aggressively I compress them, however, the easier it becomes to lose something useful. Pooling-aware training teaches the encoder to preserve the information that matters when its vectors are merged, helping you retrieve better from the same storage budget.

Industry observers note that in this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff. With pool_factor=4, my normally trained model retains 94.6% of its unpooled NanoBEIR nDCG@10, with a 4x reduction in document vectors. Token pooling-aware training raises that retention to 97.8% at the same storage budget! Let's see how.

It has been revealed that this post builds on pooling-aware training studied in Stefan Josef's Learn to Pool and LightOn's pooling regularization study, which also explores targeted training and adaptive budgets. Here, I'll focus on understanding the method and putting it to work with a short, reproducible Sentence Transformers example.

Recent findings suggest that pooling-aware training improves retrieval quality at the same vector budget. Details below.

A single-vector embedding model compresses an entire document into one vector. Multi-vector models such as ColBERT instead keep a collection of contextual token vectors, allowing different parts of a query to match different parts of a document.

For example, a query about a laptop with a long battery life can find evidence about the laptop in one part of a document and battery endurance in another. With MaxSim scoring, each query vector selects its best matching document vector, and those scores are added together:.

MaxSim⁡(Q,D)=∑q∈Qmax⁡d∈Dq⊤d \operatorname{MaxSim}(Q, D) = \sum_{q \in Q} \max_{d \in D} q^\top d MaxSim(Q,D)=q∈Q∑​d∈Dmax​q⊤d.

Recent findings suggest that even with the 2-bit or 4-bit residual quantization supported by Fast-PLAID, storing hundreds of vectors per document adds up. At 4 bits per residual coordinate, 200 vectors of 128 dimensions require 12.8 KB of quantized residuals per document, or 12.8 GB across a million documents. Pooling each document to 50 vectors reduces that to 3.2 GB, at the same dimensionality and precision.

The useful observation is that many document vectors can be similar. Several tokens might describe closely related concepts, creating an opportunity to represent them together.

In a recent development, hierarchicalTokenPooling groups similar token embeddings using Ward hierarchical clustering. Starting with one group per token vector, it repeatedly merges the two groups that cause the smallest increase in how spread out the vectors are within their groups. This spread is measured by the sum of squared distances from each vector to its group's mean, so Ward's method favors compact groups of similar vectors.

In a recent development, these merges build a hierarchy of progressively larger groups, letting us choose a level of compression that fits our budget. We then represent each group by its mean and normalize the resulting vectors again, ready for MaxSim scoring.

You can make compression proportional to document length:.

Sources indicate that with pool_factor=4, documents retain approximately one quarter of their original vectors, so longer documents can keep proportionally more capacity. By default, the first token is protected from merging and pooling applies only to document embeddings, leaving query embeddings unchanged.

HierarchicalTokenPooling offers three alternative controls:.

It has been revealed that this distinction matters when document lengths vary. With pool_factor=4, a longer document can retain approximately one quarter of its vectors, allowing its representation to grow with its content. With distance_threshold, the vector count can grow when more distinct embeddings need to be preserved.

According to recent reports, adaptive pooling uses a shared distance threshold to merge similar embeddings more aggressively while preserving more vectors for documents with distinct content. It can be used with any multi-vector model, including one trained without a pooling-aware objective.

Rather than choosing a threshold manually, you can calibrate it for a target average vector count. Given a representative sample of your corpus in calibration_documents:.

Industry observers note that calibration only needs document embeddings and returns a threshold you can reuse when indexing. The target is an average, so individual documents can receive more or fewer than 16 vectors. The achieved average can also change on another corpus.

Pooling can already be useful on an ordinary multi-vector model. The difficulty appears when a document contains a distinction that matters for retrieval, but merging its vectors makes that distinction harder to recover. The original training objective never required the model to work with these compressed representations. But, you can teach it to do exactly that.

If you've used Matryoshka embeddings, the training principle will feel familiar. Matryoshka applies a retrieval objective at several embedding widths, teaching smaller prefixes to remain useful. Pooling-aware training applies the objective to representations with fewer token vectors.

For my example, each training batch contributes two losses:.

L=12Lunpooled+12Lpooled \mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{unpooled}} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pooled}} L=21​Lunpooled​+21​Lpooled​.

The first term teaches the model to retrieve with its full representations. The second teaches it to arrange its token embeddings so that useful matches survive pooling. Both objectives update the same encoder, giving it feedback about retrieval before and after compression.

Sources indicate that ward clustering makes discrete decisions about which tokens belong together. During training, HierarchicalTokenPooling uses a straight-through estimator to pass gradients from pooled vectors back to their member tokens, without differentiating the cluster assignments. The encoder can then learn from retrieval errors made with its pooled representations.

MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss wraps an existing multi-vector retrieval loss and applies it using your chosen poolers:.

CachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss supplies the retrieval objective. It teaches each query to score its relevant document above the negative documents in the batch. By default, it uses model.similarity, using the model's similarity setting (MaxSim in this example) and kernel settings. A model configured with similarity_fn_name="meanmaxsim" would also use MeanMaxSim during training.

According to recent reports, gradient caching allows the encoder to process small mini-batches while retaining a larger set of in-batch negatives. My training script uses mini-batches of 64 with a training batch size of 256.

Recent findings suggest that multiVectorTokenPoolingLoss adds the compression objective. Here, None means that one variant uses the original embeddings, while pooling supplies the factor-4 variant. The two weights average their losses. Pooling variants reuse the computed token embeddings, so each additional pooler adds clustering and scoring work without requiring a separate encoder pass for that variant.

It has been revealed that the poolers can also be custom BaseTokenPooling implementations that preserve gradients through their input embeddings. You can adapt the training objective to the representation you want to deploy.

Replace the factor-4 pooler with your chosen deployment configuration, or include several poolers and choose weights for their losses.

Industry observers note that the complete training script includes the dataset, trainer, validation loss, and small retrieval evaluations during training. From a checkout of the repository, run both variants locally with uv:.

The script declares its training and kernel dependencies, so uv installs them for you. Compatible kernels are enabled automatically.

Industry observers note that this runs the pooling-aware variant on an A10G GPU with a four-hour time limit. Passing HF_TOKEN as a secret lets the script upload the trained model to your Hub account when training finishes. To run the ordinary-loss baseline as well, repeat the command with --baseline after the script URL.

Sources indicate that you can accelerate MaxSim scoring, Ward clustering, and supported backbone operations with kernels. Install the training and kernel dependencies:.

In the training example above, replace the model and pooler initialization before constructing the loss:.

Hierarchical poolers inherit the model's kernel settings by default, so you only need to enable kernels on the model.

Sentence Transformers selects compatible kernels for your setup and uses the existing implementation wherever a replacement isn't available. For example, the default MaxSim kernel scores queries against documents without building the full token similarity matrix in memory, but it does require CUDA and Triton.

The default Ward clustering kernel considerably speeds up hierarchical clustering by running on CUDA instead of the CPU. We're talking about 30-150x faster than SciPy depending on the setting.

Let's load the pooling-aware model and retrieve with compressed document embeddings. Kernel settings aren't saved with the model, so add use_kernels=True when loading if you'd like to use them for inference too:.

It has been revealed that the pooler compresses the document embeddings after the encoder's forward pipeline, reducing the total from 58 vectors to 16 while leaving query embeddings unchanged. Mars still receives the highest similarity score, followed by Jupiter and Venus, so the ranking is preserved despite storing far fewer document vectors.

Sources indicate that you can change pool_factor at inference to explore a different storage budget with the same trained model. For repeated use, you can also pass token_pooling=pooling when initializing MultiVectorEncoder to make it the runtime default. The pooler's tasks still control which inputs are compressed (e.g. only documents).

To investigate, I trained two models from answerdotai/ModernBERT-base, each with a fresh 128-dimensional token projection:.

Both runs use one epoch over the same 120,000 MS MARCO triplets, seed 42, and matching initialization and optimization settings. The training token cap is 300, and short queries are expanded to at least 32 token positions to provide additional contextual query vectors. Only the loss differs between the two experiments, and I didn't run a hyperparameter search.

Sources indicate that I evaluated both models on NanoBEIR@13, reporting mean nDCG@10 (%). The figure compares ordinary and pooling-aware training with pool factors of 2, 3, 4, and 6, alongside unpooled retrieval. The table also includes fixed caps and adaptive thresholds, showing how the training benefits transfer to other pooling settings.

Sources indicate that for adaptive pooling, I calibrated a separate threshold for each encoder and NanoBEIR corpus, using its unpooled document embeddings to match the average vector counts under caps of 64, 32, and 16. Short documents bring those averages below their respective caps.

It has been revealed that at the trained pool_factor=4, nDCG@10 improves from 49.03 to 51.23, while storing 74.8% fewer document vectors than unpooled retrieval. This increases score retention from 94.6% to 97.8%, where retention is the pooled mean nDCG@10 divided by each model's own unpooled mean. Unpooled retrieval also improves, from 51.84 to 52.39.

It has been revealed that the gains extend to fixed caps and adaptive pooling, even though training used only the full representation and proportional pooling. At an average of 29.58 vectors per document, adaptive pooling retains 97.3% of the pooling-aware model's unpooled score while storing 84.7% fewer document vectors. The normally trained model retains 93.3% at the same budget.

If index size is your main concern, I would reach for these options in this order:.

If the model's default dimensionality is larger than 128, I would consider Matryoshka truncation and fine-tuning earlier as well. These approaches can be combined, so evaluate the resulting index size and retrieval quality with your search engine and corpus.

Sources indicate that multiVectorMatryoshkaLoss trains token embeddings to remain useful after truncation. You can wrap it with MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss to train for both smaller dimensions and fewer document vectors, reusing the encoder's embeddings across the compression settings.

Industry observers note that try the complete training example, choose a budget that matters for your application, and compare it with a matched ordinary-loss run. The accompanying evaluation script measures unpooled retrieval, caps of 64, 32, 16, 8, and 4 vectors, and pool factors of 2 through 6, so you can plot the quality and storage tradeoff for your own model.

Sources indicate that with a few extra lines in the training objective, a smaller document representation becomes something the model actively learns to use. That opens up an exciting amount of room to make multi-vector retrieval more practical!

  • CISA, the Australian Signals Directorate’s Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD’s ACSC) and the National Security Agency (NSA) released joint guidance and an accompanying quick-reference list to help organizations assess vendor readiness for transitioning to post-quantum cryptography (PQC).
  • Sources indicate that many organizations rely on third-party vendors for managed services, cloud capabilities, and other cryptography-dependent products and services.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that CISA, the Australian Signals Directorate’s Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD’s ACSC) and the National Security Agency (NSA) released joint guidance and an accompanying quick-reference list to help organizations assess vendor readiness for transitioning to post-quantum cryptography (PQC). As quantum computing advances, widely used public-key cryptography will become vulnerable to compromise from cryptographically relevant quantum computers (CRQCs). To protect their systems and data, organizations must blueprint for and transition to PQC—which includes algorithms capable of withstanding both classical computing and quantum-enabled threats—before CRQCs become available. Many organizations rely on third-party vendors for managed services, cloud capabilities, and other cryptography-dependent products and services. Cryptography is also embedded in systems and devices that are difficult to revision, tied to long asset lifecycles, and require vendor support or replacement—such as industrial control systems and Internet of Things (IoT) devices. Reliance on vendors means that effective PQC transition depends on vendor readiness, and early, structured engagement with these vendors is critical to planning efforts. Organizations can use the vendor-neutral questions outlined in this guidance to determine whether a vendor understands quantum-related risks, maintains transparency over its cryptographic implementations, and supports a secure, cost-effective and timely transition to PQC. Visit CISA’s PQC Initiative page for additional resources.

As WIRED’s resident vacuum tester, I’ve tried every recent Dyson vacuum—from the newest, most powerful model to the long-favored V15 Detect—and I have a lot of thoughts on which ones you should buy, and at what price. The best time to shop is during sale season, and lucky for you, Dyson's Black Friday deals have already started as of today. If you’re looking to pick up a upcoming vacuum before your family comes over for Thanksgiving, here's the on-sale models I recommend.

Industry observers note that want more deals? Check out our guide to the Best Early Black Friday Deals, the Best Early Black Friday TV Deals, and the Best REI Holiday Sale Outdoor Deals.

If you want a cheaper vacuum that still comes with two cleaner heads, the older Dyson V15 Detect is also already on sale ($599), and it's even bundled with the Car Cleaning Kit, meaning three extra attachments. The V15 was our top Dyson vacuum pick for a long time because it's more affordable than the Gen5Detect and V16, but still packs two cleaner heads (the Digital Motorbar for carpet and Fluffy Optic for hard floors) and has 240 air-watts of suction (almost 100 more than the V10 Konical and other cheaper Dyson vacuums). It's a great all-around vacuum, and this bundle option gets you great extra attachments.

The PencilVac is incredibly handy and compact, and great if you're trying to do quick pickups daily on hard floors. You won't want it if you have any kind of rug or carpet, since it's only designed for hard flooring, but I did find it incredibly easy to grab and use for constant litter trails in my house. It's incredibly lightweight and a great fit for anyone with mobility or strength concerns. If these features speak to you, this is a great time to buy, as it's already on sale.

Sources indicate that this wet floor cleaner is often on sale for around $400, so it's not a huge surprise to see this deal ahead of Black Friday. The Dyson Clean+Wash is primarily a wet floor cleaner, but it can do dry cleans, too, and does not use a filter you inevitably need to keep clean. WIRED reviewer Kat Merck noticed no weird smells in three months of use. It's similar to the Dyson WashG1, with a self-propelled design that makes it easy to push around the room, and it does a good job scrubbing floors clean. Keep in mind that it's not great for dry debris, since its just rolling, not sucking.

According to recent reports, the Dyson Spot+Scrub Ai came out earlier this year and is one of my favorite robot vacuums from the brand. That's including the newer Dyson R3 Nurovi Spot+Scrub UV I’m currently testing, which hasn't blown me away as a better investment. (It actually failed my corner test completely, which vacuums in that price range should not do.).

The Spot+Scrub Ai is much lower priced, and despite some dubious AI feature claims, it does a good job cleaning autonomously. It’s often discounted around this price, but the $400-off sale is a little better than what I saw during Prime Day.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CISA has added one latest vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-19868 SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN Use of Single-factor Authentication Vulnerability This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not presently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Snapchat unveiled on Wednesday that it’s giving Lens creators the ability to build Lenses using the AI coding assistants they already use, like Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex. Snapchat Lenses, which are a core part of the social network’s platform, are AR effects that let consumers alter their appearance, add digital objects to their surroundings, or interact with animated experiences through the camera.

In a recent development, the tech giant is introducing Easy Lens CLI, which builds on its existing Easy Lens tool, which lets creators generate Lenses from a single prompt on the web and mobile. Easy Lens CLI brings that same idea into developers’ existing workflows, allowing AI assistants to handle the technical work while creators focus on the vision for the Lens itself.

The launch indicates that Snapchat is looking to lower the barrier to creating AR content, while making its platform more accessible to developers who are increasingly using AI coding assistants. Instead of requiring creators to learn how to use Snapchat’s own development tools, the tech giant is bringing Lens creation into the AI coding workflows they already use, which could in turn expand the pool of people who build for Snapchat.

Industry observers note that developers enrolled in Snapchat’s Lens+ Payouts program can earn from the Lenses they create with Easy Lens CLI. Snapchat says it paid out $1.8 million to Lens+ community creators last month.

Recent findings suggest that lens creators can describe the Lens they want in plain language, and their AI assistant handles the process from start to finish, Snapchat indicates. That includes building with more than 100 AR building blocks and 50 AI asset generators, generating previews, and publishing them to Snapchat and tracking their performance.

With Easy Lens CLI, Snapchat indicates developers can create everything from Web Lens games with leaderboards to camera effects and beauty filters.

Recent findings suggest that AI assistants can generate assets, build and test Lenses, address errors, and send updated versions directly to the creator’s phone. The latest capability can take a game from an initial idea to a published Lens in a single day, without developers having to write code themselves, Snapchat says.

The tool is aimed at different types of creators. The manufacturer notes that game developers can bring existing browser games to Snapchat as Web Lenses, while AI creators can use assets from their preferred tools to build Lenses in their own style. Additionally, agencies and brands can turn existing campaign videos, images, and other brand assets into AR experiences with less production time.

Easy Lens CLI runs on Mac, Windows, and Linux.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • CISA has added four latest vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.
  • These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-102895 GPUStack Improper Authentication Vulnerability  CVE-2026-116779 SignalWire FreeSwitch Code Injection Vulnerability  CVE-2026-123158 OpenBSD OpenSSH Unexpected Status Code or Return Value Vulnerability  CVE-2026-123218 IBM Aspera Faspex Incorrect Authorization Vulnerability  These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not at the moment listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2186 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that frontier cloud LLMs carry high operational costs that can fluctuate unexpectedly, and relying on such third-party models introduces vulnerabilities, as providers can modify, deny, or deprecate access at any time.
  • Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment.
  • Building upon the foundation of BotPsy, future development by Tether Data, S.A.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that frontier cloud LLMs carry high operational costs that can fluctuate unexpectedly, and relying on such third-party models introduces vulnerabilities, as providers can modify, deny, or deprecate access at any time. Furthermore, proprietary models offer limited customization for specific workflows, while posing risks to privacy, data control, and transparency. Besides, not every task demands frontier-level intelligence: small, specialized agents can be equally capable on specific tasks and significantly cheaper to run, since many routine or smaller workloads can be processed efficiently on-device. As intelligence per parameter continues to improve rapidly, we aim to stand at the forefront of this shift toward performant, privacy-focused, self-hosted models.

Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the Intended Use and Limitations for more information.

🤗 Model (safetensors)  |  📦 GGUFs (bf16, Q8, Q4).

Building upon the foundation of BotPsy, future development by Tether Data, S.A. de C.V. (“Tether AI Research”, “we”, “our”) will focus on expanding on-device agentic capabilities to seamlessly integrate with an even broader array of hardware and local services. Tether's Hypersearch will evolve to support more robust decentralized peer-to-peer (P2P) queries, further ensuring private, encrypted web searches that bypass corporate trackers. QVAC Fabric local fine-tuning mechanisms will be optimized to adapt more deeply to individual user preferences, workflows, and specialized tool environments. Future iterations will allow the smartphone interface to smoothly delegate heavy computational tasks to home PCs or trusted secure P2P nodes during offline-online transitions. Privacy protocols will be continuously strengthened to guarantee that all personal data, credentials, and decisions remain strictly on local hardware. Collaborative features will be introduced to allow secure agent-to-agent communication across trusted local networks without compromising user confidentiality. Ultimately, these advancements will solidify BotPsy as a fully autonomous, highly capable personal AI ecosystem that keeps owners entirely in control of their digital lives.

In a recent development, botPsy is based on Qwen3.5-0.8B and is post-trained in four sequential stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and two rounds of Reinforcement Learning (RL). Each stage uses the previous stage's best checkpoint as its starting point and benefits from a different learning signal: imitation of reference trajectories, the token distributions of much larger teacher models, and rule-based tool-calling rewards (see Figure 3).

Our approach uses four stages of training, which learn from three types of signal: demonstrations, specialist teachers, and verifiable rewards.

Learning from demonstrations (SFT).

Sources indicate that we first perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on tool-use conversations. These include multi-turn agent trajectories from simulated environments, replayed single, parallel and multi-step calls, and cases where no tool should be called.

In a recent development, next, the student is trained with on-policy distillation (OPD): it generates its own responses, and a specialist teacher provides feedback on every token, using the per-token reverse KL divergence as the training signal. To build the teachers, we first RL-trained three Qwen3.5-4B models to specialize in tool use, general reasoning, and instruction following. During training, every prompt is routed to one of these teachers. This stage mainly aims to recover knowledge and instruction following, which degraded during the SFT stage, although the tool-use metrics also increase (see Figure 4).

Learning from rules and environments (RL stages).

According to recent reports, finally, the model is trained with reinforcement learning using DAPO [1], learning only from rewards computed by rules and verifiers. The first round focuses on tool calling, accompanied by instruction following and STEM multiple-choice questions. As in Tool-N1 [2], the tool-calling reward first checks the reasoning and tool-call format. Instead of Tool-N1's binary correctness reward, however, it gives fine-grained partial credit in the spirit of ToolRL [3], matching the predicted tool names, argument names, and argument values against the ground truth.

Recent findings suggest that the second round widens the training mix to general-domain verifiable tasks: math, code, knowledge (multiple-choice) questions, instruction following, structured outputs, and multi-step tool use in a simulated workplace environment. Although this mix contains no multi-turn conversations, it further improves multi-turn function calling.

According to recent reports, each stage of training uses a different data mixture (Figure 5). The SFT stage focuses mainly on tool use and prepares the ground for the subsequent stages. The MOPD mixture combines tool-use, knowledge and instruction-following data, both to further improve function calling and to recover the general-domain regressions from the SFT stage. The first RL stage again focuses mainly on tool use, while the second RL stage shifts the balance toward general-domain data (instruction following, knowledge, math and code), keeping a smaller share of tool use.

According to recent reports, botPsy roughly doubles the tool-use performance of its Qwen3.5-0.8B base and is the strongest of the five models on five of the six agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 23.4), ACEBench (58.7 vs 30.1), τ-bench (51.5 vs 23.2), BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 1.9) and ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 30.5). On all five, it is also ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size (37.7, 55.4, 46.5, 2.8 and 41.2 respectively; see Table 1). On Claw-Eval, Qwen3.5-2B-Think leads (48.9 vs 46.5).

Recent findings suggest that table 1: Tool-use and agentic benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined; multipliers give parameter count relative to BotPsy-0.8B. The average is the unweighted mean of the six benchmarks. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

Sources indicate that tool-use training did not cost general knowledge: GPQA Diamond rises from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9, the best of the models at 1.2B parameters or below (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35.0 and 39.4; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 15.8 and 40.0). Knowledge still scales mainly with parameter count, and Qwen3.5-2B-Think scores well above (59.9 and 65.5). BotPsy is therefore designed to call tools for facts it does not know, not to serve as a knowledge model.

Industry observers note that table 2: General-knowledge benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

BotPsy is the best of the five at following explicit instructions: IFEval 90.8 (base 59.7; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 80.0) and IFBench 55.9 (base 22.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 40.9). On Multi-IF, which tests instruction following over three turns in eight languages, it scores 67.2, on par with Qwen3.5-2B-Think (66.9) and LFM2.5-1.2B-Think (68.2). It starts strongest (84.3 in turn 1, the highest of the five) but drops faster as instructions accumulate (51.0 in turn 3, vs 56.5 and 56.2 for those two models). Lower-resource languages remain a weakness: Hindi (24.5) and Russian (57.6) are far below the 72–80 reached in English, Chinese, French, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese.

Table 3: Instruction-following benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

The largest relative gains come in multi-turn, stateful interaction, where BotPsy leads four of the five multi-turn benchmarks (Figure 6). On BFCL v4 multi-turn it rises from 7.5 to 46.1, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8), and on ACEBench Agent from 7.9 to 28.3 (Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 16.2). On τ²-bench it doubles its base in retail (67.8 vs 33.9, a narrow lead over Qwen3.5-2B-Think at 65.5) and reaches 82.5 in telecom, where the agent has to guide a user through troubleshooting over many turns (MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 74.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 69.3). It is also the most reliable of the five at single calls (BFCL non-live: 83.0) and at not calling a tool when none fits (BFCL hallucination: 86.1).

Recent findings suggest that botPsy's weaker spots are open-ended search and a few areas where Qwen3.5-2B-Think still leads. BotPsy's BrowseComp-Plus score of 4.5 is the best of the five, but low in absolute terms, and on BFCL web search (14.0) and memory (16.3) it trails Qwen3.5-2B-Think (19.8 and 26.1). On Claw-Eval, BotPsy improves clearly on its base (46.5 vs 39.3) but remains slightly below Qwen3.5-2B-Think (48.9). On ACEBench's special cases (incomplete or erroneous requests), Qwen3.5-2B-Think is also ahead (58.0 vs 51.3), although BotPsy is far above its base there (13.7). τ³-banking is the one multi-turn benchmark where BotPsy does not lead: no model gets above 5 (BotPsy 4.1, unchanged from its base; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 4.8).

It has been revealed that botPsy can handle a variety of use cases and scenarios. Figure 7 breaks the benchmark scenarios down by app group, separating simple scenarios (single turn, one tool call) from complex ones (multi-turn or multi-tool). The overall scores quoted in this section are averaged over all scenarios; the bottom row of Figure 7 is an unweighted mean of the seven groups, so its numbers differ.

It has been revealed that simple scenarios score 70–79 in every app group with a meaningful sample (Communication & Social has only 6). Overall, BotPsy scores 75, about 21 points above its base model (54) and slightly above Qwen3.5-2B-Think (70).

According to recent reports, on complex scenarios, BotPsy scores 39.5 overall, against 17.9 for its base and 30.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. The gain is largest in Communication & Social (61 vs 13 for the base), Commerce & Services (58 vs 27) and Device & System Management (46 vs 15). Qwen3.5-2B-Think is ahead only in Personal Productivity & Work (64 vs 58, 38 scenarios, mostly Claw-Eval), and MiniCPM5-1B-Think is marginally ahead in Communication & Social (61.5 vs 60.5). Multi-step tasks still score lower than single calls, which remains the main limit for harder tasks.

Complex Information Retrieval & Research scenarios score 15 (single calls: 79). Most are BrowseComp-Plus deep-research questions, which stay hard for every model in this size range (base: 9; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 14).

BotPsy reaches correct answers with much less reasoning than its base, and with fewer turns on multi-turn agent tasks. This aligns with our explicit focus on reasoning efficiency throughout training. All comparisons below are made on the same questions or tasks (those that all five models answered correctly or solved), so differences in difficulty do not drive the numbers. Reasoning tokens are counted with each model's own tokenizer.

Shorter reasoning, with higher accuracy. Compared with its base, BotPsy uses 1.4–3.1× fewer reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563), MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105), IFEval (3,148 vs 4,433) and IFBench (4,204 vs 11,576), while scoring higher on all four (Figure 8). It is not the shortest model everywhere: LFM2.5-1.2B-Think writes shorter reasoning on MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench, and MiniCPM5-1B-Think on IFEval and IFBench, but at lower accuracy than BotPsy on each.

Sources indicate that fewer turns than the base on multi-turn agent tasks. On τ²-bench tasks that all five models solve, BotPsy needs fewer assistant turns than its base (Figure 9):.

Sources indicate that it does this while passing 2.0× (retail) and 2.6× (telecom) as many tasks as the base. MiniCPM5-1B-Think uses fewer turns on retail (8.7), but passes only 9.9% of retail tasks.

Industry observers note that botPsy has been developed to advance the state of the art and to support research and educational uses. Models developed based on our work could be suitable for tasks in domains such as device & system management (settings, files & documents, clocks & alarms), personal productivity & work (calendar & tasks, email, collaboration tools), communication (messaging), information retrieval & research (web search, weather, news), media & lifestyle (video, music, recipes & fitness, photos) and commerce & services (maps & travel, finance, shopping & delivery). Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty.

BotPsy has been primarily trained and tested in English, which is the recommended language. It has also been evaluated on Multi-IF, which covers seven additional languages (Chinese, French, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish): it performs well in most of them, but scores much lower in Hindi and Russian. BotPsy is a small language model, and it makes mistakes. It is not intended for safety-critical or high-stakes automated decisions, or for applications involving money, personal information, health and other sensitive topics.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stephen Quinn joined the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in 2004 and serves as a senior computer scientist in the Information Technology Laboratory (ITL).
  • Industry observers note that stephen was named to the “Federal 100” by the trade publication Federal Computer Week (FCW) and received the Department of Commence Gold Medal Award for his work in automating security protocols for applications.

Mr. Stephen Quinn joined the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in 2004 and serves as a senior computer scientist in the Information Technology Laboratory (ITL). Mr. Quinn is the lead author for Integrating NIST risk management project work within the paradigm of Enterprise Risk Management (ERM). He is also program manager for the National Checklist Program and the National Online Informative Reference (OLIR) programs at NIST. He is a co-originator of the NIST Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP).

Industry observers note that stephen was named to the “Federal 100” by the trade publication Federal Computer Week (FCW) and received the Department of Commence Gold Medal Award for his work in automating security protocols for applications. He also received the Federal CIO Council Leadership award for related work.

In a recent development, prior to joining NIST, Steve worked in the private sector as a consultant to the Department of Defense and large commercial outsourcings with Wall Street banking firms and insurance companies. Specifically, he comes from an operational background, having owned two companies that provided service offering for vulnerability assessments, designing security architectures, code development, risk management, certifications and accreditations, and ST&Es. His research experience and practitioner experience includes managing and remediating risks specific to computer viruses/malware, intrusion detection systems (IDSs), vulnerability/misconfiguration identification, categorization, and remediation.

Sam Altman says his life is so weird that he’s unfazed by Andrew Garfield portraying him in upcoming movie

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hollywood has found plenty of material and cinematic inspiration from a string of Silicon Valley scandals and power struggles in recent years.
  • “You Can See Everything,” the documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, smashed box office expectations, and Netflix’s limited series “The Altruists” comes out Thursday to tell the story of Sam Bankman-Fried and the downfall of FTX.
  • As the founder and CEO of OpenAI, one of the most influential companies of the century, Sam Altman isn’t going to escape the Hollywood treatment, either.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hollywood has found plenty of material and cinematic inspiration from a string of Silicon Valley scandals and power struggles in recent years.

“You Can See Everything,” the documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, smashed box office expectations, and Netflix’s limited series “The Altruists” comes out Thursday to tell the story of Sam Bankman-Fried and the downfall of FTX.

As the founder and CEO of OpenAI, one of the most influential companies of the century, Sam Altman isn’t going to escape the Hollywood treatment, either.

In “Artificial,” a biographical comedy-drama opening in theaters on Christmas, the lauded actor Andrew Garfield will portray Altman in a film that chronicles OpenAI’s rise and the internal turmoil that erupted when he was briefly ousted in 2023.

“If you had told me 20 years ago that someone was going to make a movie about me, I think that would have struck me as … that would have been a very weird thing,” Altman noted onstage at the New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday. “Now it doesn’t feel like it’s in like the top 10 weirdest things about my life.”.

Industry observers note that garfield is best known for his role as Spider-Man, but his big break came in 2010, when he played Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin in “The Social Network” alongside Jesse Eisenberg as Mark Zuckerberg. (That film also had a sequel of sorts this year called “The Social Reckoning,” but it bombed at the box office.).

So, if Altman isn’t fazed by the looming release of “Artificial,” what’s actually the weirdest thing in his life?

“The fact that we are ushering in this technology that we have all of these very real concerns about, and that we have, we find ourselves in a role of such significance and such responsibility to make that go well,” Altman stated. “That’s a crazy situation to find yourself in.”.

Sure, that is pretty weird, Sam. It’s also weird that you use ChatGPT for parenting advice and don’t respect olive oil. But I’d wager to say it’s even weirder that there’s an upcoming film about the time your colleagues briefly ousted you because they were concerned that you can’t be trusted.

Say what you want about Mark Zuckerberg (I certainly have), but at least he’s honest about what he thinks about “The Social Network.”.

“It was weird, man,” Zuckerberg reflected on a podcast last year. “They got all these very specific details of what I was wearing, or these specific things correct, but then the whole narrative arc around my motivations and all this stuff were like, completely wrong … The whole arc is like, I’m somehow motivated by trying to find a girlfriend, [but] I was dating Priscilla [Chan] before I started Facebook.”.

Zuckerberg said he knew his employees would be tempted to see the movie, so he organized a company outing when it was released, even though the film hardly paints a flattering portrait of him.

Zuckerberg even had enough of a sense of humor to buy a prop from the film at auction. He owns an Ardsley High School T-shirt that Eisenberg wore in the movie and even wore it himself in a video with YouTubers Colin and Samir.

Eisenberg hasn’t been particularly complimentary of Zuckerberg, saying that he doesn’t want to think of himself as “associated with somebody like that.” And while “Artificial” hasn’t hit theaters yet, Garfield doesn’t seem to have a much more favorable opinion of the tech founder he portrays.

Sources indicate that “I don’t know Sam Altman. I’ve never met him,” Garfield told Esquire. “But I think anyone who takes on that level of responsibility for a organization or technology that you know is going to do a hell of a lot of damage to the soul of humanity [must have] a certain ability to dissociate.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Josh and Jason are building the data and deployment layer for physical AI.
  • Josh and Jason are building the data and deployment layer for physical AI.
  • AI took the digital world by storm in a few short years, and we are still only scratching the surface.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Josh and Jason are building the data and deployment layer for physical AI.

Josh and Jason are building the data and deployment layer for physical AI.

AI took the digital world by storm in a few short years, and we are still only scratching the surface. Each time digital AI has moved to a new phase, from pretraining to reinforcement learning to deployment, spend on compute and data has not plateaued. It has accelerated.

Sources indicate that bringing AI into the physical world will be a wave of comparable importance to digital AI, if not larger, but the infrastructure required to get there will be harder to build and scale, and that already demonstrates at every stage. In pretraining, language models benefited from decades of text accumulated on the internet. Robotics has no comparable, ready-made collection of the movements, interactions and sensory information needed to understand the physical world. That experience has to be captured before it can be learned from. In reinforcement learning and deployment, digital AI operates in clean, structured environments that are easy to scale. Physical AI lives in the noisy, unpredictable, operationally complex reality of the real world. It operates in the field, not in the cloud.

To reach physical AGI, the industry has to build both the brain and the body. The brain needs data that wasnât collected. The body needs someone doing the work on the ground.

That is the mission Josh, Jason and the Mecka AI team have taken on: helping physical AI labs, robotics companies and end enterprises reach physical AGI and put it to use, by being their partner for training data, reinforcement learning, and deployment.

Delivering on this mission requires developing several muscles across disciplines, all at once and all at scale:.

Research: Identify the next wave in robotics, and what it will require, before it arrives.

Hardware: Once you see the wave, design the bespoke hardware and wearables to capture the data, then manufacture them fast, economically, and at scale.

Operations: Run large-scale global operations to collect the data. Volume alone is not enough; the data has to span every job in every industry.

Software and digital AI: Turn the raw output, which is far more voluminous and complex than text (e.g., multi-camera video, body and hand tracking, sensor streams), into high-quality, training-ready data.

Deployment: Put robots in front of end customers, for reinforcement learning and production deployment.

Recent findings suggest that each of these muscles is difficult to develop on its own, but to win, you need not one but all of them, working together and at scale. Training data today, for example, has to be high volume AND high diversity AND high quality AND delivered fast AND at a good price. It is easy to do one of these at small volume, but it is incredibly difficult to do all of them at once and at scale, and that is what it takes to help partners reach physical AGI. In the same way, it is easy to start a food delivery business that delivers a single dish from one restaurant to one apartment block, but it is incredibly difficult to scale it into a DoorDash.

Mecka's founders and team understood this and moved fast to build all five muscles, finding differentiated edge in each and executing on it. The result is a strong, scalable and flexible platform that has enabled them to win over many of the leading AI labs and robotics companies and quickly become the emerging leader of this category.

What drew us to Mecka is not that they made the right bet on the right form of data (although they did). Robotics is still early relative to digital AI. The form factor of the data might change. The form factor of the robots might change. What matters is that they built the machine that scales with the industry and its partners; regardless of how the input changes over time, the output will be what their partners want. In the same way, DoorDash built a system where, whether the input is a pizza or a laptop, the customer gets the same delightful delivery experience. And when something in the physical world has high barriers to scale, it is an opportunity for the right team to build a large, durable business with moats.

According to recent reports, that is why we are excited to back Josh, Jason and their fast-growing team. We see in them the special ingredients that will keep compounding over the long term to win this category and help their partners advance the mission of building and deploying robots at scale around the world.

And it is why others have joined us, from strategics like NVIDIA, Samsung, Microsoft and Qualcomm to the founders and operators who scaled some of the most defining companies of their generation and excel in many of the disciplines required in Meckaâs business: Tony Xu, founder and CEO of DoorDash; Frank Slootman, former CEO of ServiceNow and Snowflake; Milan Kovac, former head of Optimus at Tesla; Christopher Payne, former President & COO of Doordash; Jonathan Chadwick, former COO and CFO of VMware and board member at Databricks; and many more.Photo by S72 Business Portraits.
